title: Grace to a broken women part 3
scripture_text: ‘’Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. At dawn he appeared again in the temple courts, where all the people gathered around him, and he sat down to teach them. The teachers of the law and the Pharisees brought in a woman caught in adultery. They made her stand before the group and said to Jesus, “Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery. In the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. Now what do you say?” They were using this question as a trap, in order to have a basis for accusing him. But Jesus bent down and started to write on the ground with his finger. When they kept on questioning him, he straightened up and said to them, “Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground. At this, those who heard began to go away one at a time, the older ones first, until only Jesus was left, with the woman still standing there. Jesus straightened up and asked her, “Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?” “No one, sir,” she said. “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Go now and leave your life of sin.”
devotional:
The religious leaders

The members of the Sanhedrin have gone home, frustrated and angry that they can neither silence Jesus nor even manage to arrest Him. They are also deadlocked over how to deal with Him.

When the council members go to their own homes, Jesus and His disciples go to the Mount of Olives. Jesus also goes there in the latter days of His ministry to avoid being an easy target for assassination or arrest (see Luke 19:37; 22:39). Early in the morning, Jesus makes His way to the temple again. The people begin to gather around him, forming a crowd, and he begins to teach them.

Setting the scene.

'Caught in an act of adultery' says the writer. That was when the doors burst open. The covers jerked back. “This is not your husband” shout the fearsome looking men, as they bare down on the frightened woman. “Put on some clothes, we know how to deal with the likes of you.” And they do. So she is dragged from the moment of private passion in the bedroom to become a public spectacle in the streets. The woman clutches a thin robe to hide her nakedness, but nothing can hide her shame. From this moment on, her life will never be the same again. When she goes to the shops, women will point and whisper. When she walks down the street heads will turn. When her name is mentioned people will remember this moment. And so she is paraded through the town until they reach the temple and there she is hurled before Jesus. In fear, shame and brokenness, she awaits her condemnation.

Think of the shame this lady must had been feeling.

The Oxford English Dictionary defines shame as a ‘painful emotion arising from the consciousness of something dishonouring, ridiculous or indecorous in one's own conduct or circumstances, or of being in a situation which offends one's sense of modesty or decency.’

As this lady stood before Jesus she may well have been feeling all these things, she was probably an emotional wreck.

But there is more going on here than simply shaming and blaming a sinful woman. The men who threw her at Jesus’ feet had a hidden agenda. Things were not as they seemed. These religious leaders didn’t care about the woman nor on this occasion did they care about the law. They simply wanted to ‘test’ (peirazo- often translated as ‘tempt’) Jesus, so that they might have grounds for accusing him. In other words, their prior overt tactics had failed to silence Jesus, so now they resorted to a more crafty and subtle approach.

The attitude of the religious leaders.

It is important that we grasp the heart attitudes of these religious leaders as they drag this poor women into their conflict with Jesus.

They manipulated scripture to affirm their judgmental attitude.

They tried to cover their own sins by exposing the sin of others. Would we ever do that?

The required judgment.

The Old Testament listed adultery as a capital crime (Lev. 20:10). This is horrifying to the modern reader, where it merits no punishment in our society. Though we are no longer under Old Testament civil law, it is not difficult to understand why adultery could lead to such serious judgment, especially when compared to the other ancient Near Eastern law codes. The Mosaic law was very tough on crimes against people, relationships, and the family unit. The other law codes were very tough on property crimes – for example, cutting off hands for stealing. This difference highlights the contrasting value-systems of the people of God and those around them – of prioritising people versus things.

The religious leaders hoped to impale Jesus on the horns of a dilemma. If he agreed with the Old Testament law and called for her execution, they could accuse him of sedition before the Romans, because since 30 AD the Romans had taken away the Jews' right of capital punishment. However, if he said she shouldn't be stoned, they could accuse him of false teaching and discredit him with the people.

The Old Testament law mandated that to be prosecuted, adulterers needed to be caught in the act (Num. 5:13). Rabbi Samuel said, "In the case of adulterers, they (the witnesses) must have seen them in the posture of adulterers."Another scholar of Talmudic law says, "(It is not just an issue) of their having seen the couple in a `compromising situation,' for example, coming from a room in which they were alone, or even lying together on the same bed. The actual physical movements of the couple must have been capable of no other explanation, and the witnesses must have seen exactly the same acts at exactly the same time, in the presence of each other, so that their depositions would be identical in every respect."

As we read the account of this story in John, we see that the religious leaders tell Jesus that the woman had indeed been caught ‘in the very act of adultery’. It seems that they have been conscientious in their compliance with the detail of the Torah. However, their adherence to the law was selective and flawed.

The Torah also stated that both parties were to be produced and prosecuted (Deut. 22:22). If they caught the woman ‘in the very act,’ then where is the man? It is obvious that there is a conspiracy here! The whole story could have been fabricated, but the most plausible explanation is that these men have set the woman up to use her in their attempt to discredit Jesus.

They may have sent an ‘undercover agent’ to solicit the woman’s services (maybe even one of their own number), then on a pre-arranged signal, they burst in, let him go and dragged her to Jesus. This makes them accessories to the crime and therefore guilty of adultery themselves!
prayer: Father is there any condemnation in my heart towards others?
